recommendations.name: Win-loss program
recommendations.purpose: Run the recurring win/loss program: CRM loss-reason check, neutral buyer interviews and a coded, triangulated readout. Each theme is routed to positioning, pricing, CI, ICP or enablement.
recommendations.why: Four kit skills use win-loss evidence and none produces it. positioning-and-messaging says 'where win-loss quotes exist, read them first'. competitive-intelligence's battlecard needs a '90-day deal-intel pane with the latest win, loss, and at-risk quotes'. The merged icp-and-segmentation compares won/lost/churned accounts. field-enablement's sourced-proof rule needs real objections. competitive-intelligence only has 'win-loss' as a trigger and folds in quotes 'where they exist'. Teammates cover only fragments: Omar's lost-deal-analysis reads CRM reason codes, and Max's voice-of-customer-loop has a single win-loss paragraph aimed at product. Owning win/loss analyses sits beside battlecards in GTM strategy and PMM role definitions. It appears as a Win/Loss section in alirezarezvani's marketing-strategy-pmm (MIT) and as a pm-pmm skill in the upstream below. The upstream is verified MIT at a pinned commit, 103 lines plus references/buyer-interview-craft.md. It already has a normalized reason taxonomy, controllable-vs-structural split, per-cut win rates and a no-fabricated-quotes rule. It needs the AutoGPT adaptations sketched below.

source.ref: mohitagw15856/pm-claude-skills skills/win-loss-analysis (SKILL.md + references/buyer-interview-craft.md) @ f6ca79348c5518f1b0e8bcfd6da53b61251c0fa2

sketch: Inputs and data check: closed-won, closed-lost and no-decision deals from HubSpot via run_block or an export. First run Omar's reason-quality test: if more than 25% of reasons are blank, 'other' or back-filled, flag that before any cut. Gong has no block, so transcripts are pasted or come through a connected MCP.

Interview program: a neutral interviewer (never the owning rep), 2-6 weeks after the decision, half wins and half losses, about 5 per quarter. Keep the upstream guide in references/buyer-interview-craft.md. Recruiting emails are drafted in Gmail and wait for the owner's yes, and any incentive is a budget ask.

Coding and math in bash_exec: a fixed taxonomy that includes no-decision; stated reason vs first-mentioned anxiety; win rate by segment, competitor, source and size, each with its n. Any cut under about 30 deals is flagged as noise, matching the gtm-performance-diagnostics rule.

Triangulation bar before anything changes (from Max's VOC loop): buyer, seller and CRM evidence across 3 or more deals. Every line is labeled FACT, INFERENCE or UNKNOWN, and every quote is verbatim with its deal id.

Routing table: alternatives and value go to positioning-and-messaging; 'price' losses go to pricing-and-packaging as a value-perception read; competitor patterns go to the competitive-intelligence battlecard diff; fit patterns go to icp-and-segmentation; objections go to field-enablement-content; product gaps go to Max's voice-of-customer-loop or Alex.

Output: a quarterly readout saved dated under win-loss/, with each action added to the decision log. The competitor-brief routine's rep-corroboration line reads from this log. Move the 'win-loss' trigger here from competitive-intelligence.

recommendations.name: Demand and pipeline plan
recommendations.purpose: Turn the period's bookings target into time-phased pipeline and lead targets by month, segment and source, with cycle lag, capacity and feasibility checked. These become the targets the scorecard grades against.
recommendations.why: The weekly GTM scorecard routine and day_one 'Your GTM funnel, scored' grade every metric R/Y/G 'against target'. No skill produces those targets. gtm-performance-diagnostics says 'No targets means you propose them from history' (PROPOSED in the merge), and Maya's weekly-marketing-read says 'No plan targets: skip goal against actual… ask for targets once'. Existing math stops short. diagnostics has one single-period 'backward funnel math' line. gtm-planning-and-market-entry fixes one objective number and a coverage check. The merged opportunity-sizing-and-business-case is flagged as 'still needs a time-phased model'. A grep for waterfall, time-phased or pipeline-target math finds nothing else in the catalog. This is core GTM strategy and planning work. At-Bay's Director, GTM Strategy & Operations posting lists 'translating growth objectives into capacity, pipeline, bookings, and revenue plans' and 'own… pipeline, bookings, and revenue models'. The SiriusDecisions/Forrester demand waterfall is the standard frame. Candidates checked and rejected: pm-claude-skills marketing-funnel-plan (MIT) is an untimed AARRR tactic map. alirezarezvani commercial-forecaster (MIT) forecasts existing pipeline rather than planning targets backward. So this is new, and it fits bash_exec plus the Sheets block.

source.ref: new; optionally reuse alirezarezvani/claude-skills commercial/skills/commercial-forecaster/scripts/funnel_confidence_scorer.py (MIT @19392f7) for per-stage rate confidence

sketch: Inputs: the bookings or new-ARR target by period and segment from gtm-planning's objective, plus stage conversion rates, ASP and cycle days from HubSpot or an export (window and n stated). Add the source mix (marketing, sales, partner, self-serve) and rep capacity from Max's sales-ops-coverage-and-quota. Anything missing is ASSUMED and labeled INFERENCE.

Reverse waterfall in scripts/waterfall.py (bash_exec): target ÷ ASP = wins; ÷ win rate = opportunities; ÷ SQL→opp, MQL→SQL and so on, down to leads. Each is shifted back by stage cycle time, so pipeline is dated to when it must be created, not when it closes. Output a monthly CSV, and a sheet when Sheets is connected.

Feasibility: required volume per source vs trailing actuals, with the gap named in units and currency. Levers are ranked (conversion, volume, ASP, cycle) with a ±20% sensitivity on the two weakest rates. Any rate resting on fewer than about 30 observations is marked noise.
Capacity cross-check: required opportunities per rep vs Max's ramp-adjusted capacity. A plan that cannot be staffed is a risk line, not a target.

Targets stay PROPOSED (INFERENCE) until the owner says yes. They are then written to the metrics history the weekly scorecard reads, logged in the decision log, and handed to Maya as channel volume targets. Daniel checks CAC and budget implications.

recommendations.name: Claims and proof library
recommendations.purpose: Keep one register of every claim, proof point, customer quote, logo and reference that GTM assets may use, each with its source, evidence grade, approval, permission and review date. Check drafts and launch gates against it.
recommendations.why: The persona's central boundary is 'never invent a metric, a customer name, a quote… every load-bearing claim is labeled FACT, INFERENCE, or UNKNOWN'. The review found that five kit skills never state the labelling rule. The merged field-enablement-content adds a 'sourced-proof rule', and the merged commercial-launch-strategy gate gains a 'legal/claims' item that routines[1] scores. Neither has a register to check against, so each positioning doc keeps its own ad-hoc 'claims you will never make' list. The catalog only checks claims per draft: marketing-copy-editing, channel-draft-shapes, ad-copy-variants and Maya's messaging-and-tone-matrix. None keeps permissions or expiry. External standards call for this discipline: the FTC Policy Statement Regarding Advertising Substantiation requires a reasonable basis before a claim is made; the FTC Endorsement Guides (16 CFR 255) cover testimonials; EU Directive 2006/114/EC covers comparative claims. Using a customer logo or quote needs recorded permission. No public skill with a clean licence was found, so this is new. It fits the Sheets and workspace-file tools with an approval flow.

source.ref: new

sketch: Register schema (templates/claims-register.csv, and a sheet when Sheets is connected): claim text, type (quantified, comparative, superlative, quote, logo, certification), source link and date, FACT or INFERENCE grade, owner, approver and approval date, allowed channels, review-by date.

Reference pool: which customer agreed to what (logo, quote, case study, reference call), when, and through whom, with a usage count and cap. No customer name appears in any asset without a recorded permission row.

Sweep in bash_exec: scan positioning, battlecard, launch and enablement files for numbers, superlatives and customer names, then match them to the register. Unregistered or expired claims come back as a blocking list.
Comparative claims: each needs a dated competitor source from competitive-intelligence. An 'act' move in the competitor brief expires the affected claims for re-check.

Gate hook: commercial-launch-strategy's legal/claims item passes only when every claim in the launch assets is registered, current and approved. Legal questions go to counsel (Ellis or Lena), and Zara never gives legal advice.

recommendations.name: Customer insight research
recommendations.purpose: Gather and synthesize buyer evidence (interviews, surveys, review and community mining, JTBD extraction, personas) with confidence grading. It supplies positioning and ICP with verbatim customer language.
recommendations.why: The day-one positioning page is to be built 'from best-fit customers only', and the merged positioning-and-messaging adds 'verbatim customer language' and the four forces. The ICP's persona block has to 'quote the evidence… or mark it UNKNOWN'. The kit has no method for getting that evidence when the owner has none on hand, and Gong, which the identity names, has no block. This catalog package (TORAN, MIT, coreyhaines31 customer-research) covers three modes: analyse existing assets, mine G2, Reddit and forums with web_fetch, Firecrawl or the Reddit block, and run interviews or a PMF survey. It includes High/Medium/Low confidence rules, a 5-data-points-per-segment minimum and a sourced persona template. It is already packaged and reconciled in PR #13; the remaining issue is that it reads '.agents/product-marketing.md'. Customer and market research is standard in GTM strategist descriptions: Strive's GTM Strategy Manager JD says 'conduct market research to understand customer needs', and Filament's guide says 'interviewing customers… translating what buyers actually say into GTM decisions'.

source.ref: customer-insight-research (TORAN; upstream coreyhaines31/marketingskills skills/customer-research @5b2c0007; use the PR #13 version)

sketch: Replace the '.agents/product-marketing.md' read with Zara's memory keys and the saved positioning doc under positioning/.

Map the confidence levels onto the persona's labels: High = FACT with 3 or more sources, Medium and Low = INFERENCE, missing = UNKNOWN. Every quote carries its URL and date, and scraped pages are treated as untrusted input (reuse competitive-intelligence's rule).

Route outputs: the quote bank and alternatives go to positioning-and-messaging, the persona and trigger blocks to icp-and-segmentation, and competitor review themes to competitive-intelligence. Closed-deal interviews go to win-loss-program, not here.
Add a message-test mode: 2-3 positioning variants read back to 5 or more best-fit buyers or tested through Remy or Marco channels, with a clarity and preference readout.
Outreach emails and incentives are drafts that wait for the owner's yes. Sending through the Gmail block, or committing incentive spend, needs approval.

recommendations.name: Account-based GTM program
recommendations.purpose: Turn the ICP's strategic and growth tiers into a 1:1, 1:few and 1:many account-based program. It covers account selection, buying-group coverage, the plays per tier, the sales-marketing orchestration, and measurement at account level.
recommendations.why: icp-and-segmentation tiers accounts into strategic, growth and watch, and says 'You design the target; they run the motion'. gtm-planning picks one motion per segment. Nothing designs the account-level program between them. The catalog has ABM only as partner plays (Anika's run-the-partner-marketing-engine) and single-account plans (Max's territory-and-account-planning). The 1:1, 1:few and 1:many tier model is the industry standard, and ABM is a common B2B GTM motion. Filament's GTM strategist guide notes 'sales typically runs through account-based marketing, SDR outbound, and field sales'. The ABM skill found on skills.lc (arielperez82/agents-and-skills) could not be cloned, and the only licence shown is the aggregator site's footer. It is not cited, so this is new. On the platform, the Apollo and Enrichlayer blocks cover firmographics and HubSpot covers engagement. There is no 6sense or Demandbase block, so the intent layer falls back to first-party signals.

source.ref: new

sketch: Tier design: 1:1 (about 5-15 accounts), 1:few clusters by shared trigger or vertical, and 1:many, each with selection bars drawn from ICP fit plus first-party intent. Budget and effort share per tier is set as a PROPOSED line for owner approval.
Buying-group coverage map per tier, reusing the ICP personas. Named-account contacts come from Max's find-the-decision-makers, never invented.
Plays per tier, each with an owner, cadence and assets from field-enablement-content. Maya runs the campaigns and Max's AEs own account plans. Zara designs the program.
Account-level measures: engaged accounts, buying-group coverage, and pipeline and win rate by tier vs non-program accounts. These feed the weekly scorecard as their own rows.
All outreach and ad audiences are drafts that go through the owner's approval. Intent data is used only when a connected source provides it.

roster.summary: Across the 32 experts there are three role pairs that do the same job: Alex and Priya (both "Product Manager"), Harper and Sofia (both "Recruiter") and Kai and Frankie (both "Executive Assistant"). Robin and Sasha are close to a fourth pair; their support taglines are nearly identical. My recommendations: merge Frankie into Kai (Frankie has 0 skills and a routine copied from James); merge Harper into Sofia and converge their two script sets, which have drifted apart; turn Priya into a user researcher, which also fills a gap in the roster; and split Robin and Sasha by company stage (Robin retitled Support Lead, Sasha the first support hire). The bigger cost is jobs that many experts each do their own way. Four competitor-watch routines read the same Tier 1/2/3 watch list, and Maya's and Nadia's run at the same Friday 8am slot. "go/no-go" is a trigger in three launch skills. Pipeline coverage is defined three ways across five experts. Eight Monday-morning metric reads all trigger on "here are the numbers". Three escalation briefs (counsel, compliance, HR) are nearly the same. And the same upstream package is grafted into a different base in two to four kits: sales-pipeline-review into 3, customer-response-drafting into 3, competitor-profiling into 3, product-marketing-context into 4, board-deck-builder into 2, operational-risk-assessment into 3. Each of these jobs should have one owner and one shared slug. On kit size, Max (26) and Anika (29) are still over 25 even after their proposals. Jules and Remy (3 each) are too thin unless they take their channel's work back from Maya, and Frankie has no skills at all. Roles users would expect but won't find: a growth/PLG marketer, an SDR split out of Max, a DevOps/incident lead, a designer (the catalog has no design skills), and IT/systems admin.

anika__c2-partner-sourcing.name: Source and qualify partners
anika__c2-partner-sourcing.description: Use when the user wants partner prospects found or vetted: a cited long list from account overlap, public research and investor or accelerator portfolios, scored on fit, evidence and access, qualified on partner-side criteria, with kill decisions named.
triggers: go or no-go on a partner

sections.heading: # Source and qualify partners
sections.text:
Use this when the user wants a ranked list of partner prospects, research on a candidate firm, or a go/no-go qualification. Names come from three places: account overlap against partner-side records, public research and the owner's own network, and investor or accelerator portfolios.

The job ends at a cited, scored shortlist with the kills named. Drafting the first touch belongs to partner-first-touch-outreach, and technical fit for an integration to scope-the-tech-partnership. Nothing here contacts a firm, a founder, or a portfolio company.

sections.heading: ## Inputs
## Research guardrails
sections.text:
Read these first, every time. They apply to every channel.

1. **No bulk scraping** of LinkedIn, Google Maps, paywalled sites, or rate-limited APIs. The browser is an assisted research tool, not a scraper. Extraction tools may read a firm's own website; never point them at the platforms that list firms.
2. **No CAPTCHA, login-wall, or bot-protection bypass.** If a site requires it, work with what is publicly visible.
3. **Public business contact channels only:** generic addresses (info@, hello@, contact@) and named-role addresses published on the firm's own site. Personal or private addresses need a lawful basis, such as an existing relationship or an opt-in. Never build an address from a naming pattern; where none is published, name the role and the research gap.
4. **Source URL and date for every contact**, captured and kept. Downstream outreach compliance depends on that lineage.
5. **No breached, leaked, or unprovenanced data:** no breached datasets, scraped-contact marketplaces, or list brokers with no source lineage. Licensed data providers used within their terms and with a lawful basis are fine.
6. **Never target or infer sensitive traits.** Do not qualify, segment, or personalise on health, financial hardship, political belief, sexuality, religion, or other protected or sensitive attributes, even when a public post reveals them.

No outreach to a firm, a founder, or a portfolio company goes out without the owner's explicit yes.

sections.heading: ## Procedure
sections.text: Run the steps in order. A request about one named firm runs steps 3 to 6 for that firm alone.

sections.heading: ### 1. Confirm the profile and the channels
sections.text:
Confirm the profile, the partner types, the geographies, and the target count. No profile on file means you draft one first and say so.

Decide which channels are in scope: account overlap (step 2), public research and the owner's network (step 3), and investors and accelerators (see Sourcing through investors and accelerators). Name the channels you ran in the search parameters.

sections.heading: ### 2. Map accounts before you list firms
sections.text:
Pull account and contact overlaps against partner-side records wherever they are available, and prioritise accounts that sit in their book and not in ours, sized by overlap and deal size. Match lists in the sandbox, by domain.

No partner-side records: ask for an export or a paste of the partner's account list. If there is none, say so and carry on with step 3.

origin.heading: Map accounts before you list firms

sections.heading: ### 3. Build and enrich the long list
sections.text:
Only then build the long list from public research and the owner's own network: firms matching the profile's firmographics and capabilities. Add portfolio companies when the investor channel is in scope. Source two to three times the target count; qualification culls hard.

Research with web search and each firm's own pages. Use an enrichment integration only when it is already connected.

Enrich each name with citations: what they do, who they serve, and the evidence of fit. A firm with no evidence line is a research task, not a list row.

origin.heading: Map accounts before you list firms

sections.heading: ### 4. Score, rank, and tier
sections.text:
Score every candidate on three axes: fit against the profile, evidence (how strong the proof is), and access (whether there is a warm path or a named contact). Write the scale you used at the top, as an assumption, unless the owner already has one. Rank them, and tier past roughly twenty-five names so the list stays workable.

Skip any firm already touched unless the owner says otherwise. Tag each lead partner-qualified (net-new, no introduction yet) or partner-recommended (warm introduction made, higher conversion), so pipeline reads the two differently later.

Give every row a confidence level:

- **High:** confirmed by at least two independent sources, or by the firm's official page.
- **Medium:** one credible source plus consistent search evidence.
- **Low:** incomplete or ambiguous evidence. Name what remains uncertain.

Two of your own searches are not two independent sources.

sections.heading: ### 5. Qualify the top tier
sections.text:
Run a scorecard on the top tier: audience overlap, complementary offer, sales motion match, no fatal conflict, network-overlap vetting (their book must not oversaturate our turf), and a named internal champion for the pursuit. Every line carries FACT, INFERENCE, or UNKNOWN.

Fit is not the same as qualified. Before anything gets signed, qualify the partner side, for the top tier and for any inbound partner referral:

- **Capacity:** can they resource the motion.
- **Commitment:** is there evidence they will invest in it.
- **Compatibility:** do their motion, customers, and way of working fit ours.
- **Partner economics:** does the motion make money for them.

Give each a High, Medium, or Low confidence score on the definitions in step 4. An unverified line stays UNKNOWN; it never counts as a pass.

sections.heading: ### 6. Decide: keep, kill, or park
sections.text:
Kill criteria decide. A failed fatal check kills that pursuit, not the whole list, and the kill gets written down with its reason.

A candidate that is not ready but has not failed is parked with a dated revisit trigger, not left to a slow fade.

sections.heading: ### 7. Check, hand back, and log
sections.text:
Run the self-check, then hand back the shortlist in the format below. Save the shortlist, its scores, and the kill and park decisions to the log with today's date, so the next pass can say what warmed and what stalled.

Stop there. The first move per survivor is a recommendation; any first touch is drafted through partner-first-touch-outreach and waits on the owner's yes.

sections.heading: ## Sourcing through investors and accelerators
sections.text:
Use this channel when names should come through venture capital or private equity firms, accelerators, or their portfolios.

**Build the investor map.** The firms, their theses, the portfolio fits, and the warm path per firm: who we know, evidenced, never invented. Rank by portfolio fit multiplied by reachability. No path means research, not outreach.

**Set the portfolio play.** A commercial target per portfolio (referrals, sourced pipeline, technology evaluations), the referral motion (portfolio introduction days, founder briefings, co-selling with portfolio companies), and the dated first touch per firm, staged as a draft.

**Run portfolio candidates through steps 4 to 6.** The call is convert or park, with a date on it; a parked candidate gets its revisit trigger. Technical fit for an integration goes to scope-the-tech-partnership.

**Report per portfolio monthly.** Introductions made, evaluations opened, referrals converted, and pipeline sourced. Every number names its portfolio and its window before the count, and pipeline counts carry the sourced-or-influenced proof that track-partner-pipeline defines. If the owner wants the report on a schedule, offer it as a monthly routine; it stays off until they say yes.

sections.heading: ## What you hand back
sections.text:
The ranked, scored shortlist with its evidence, the kill decisions named, and the single best first move per surviving name. Assumptions sit at the top; every load-bearing line carries FACT, INFERENCE, or UNKNOWN with its source. Firm names and titles stay exactly as the source wrote them.

**Shortlist columns**, rows in rank order: score, firm, domain, partner type, tag (partner-qualified or partner-recommended), why (cited), source URLs, confidence, last verified date, first move.

**Format.** A markdown table in chat up to 25 rows. Above 25 rows, or when the owner asks for a file, write a CSV to the workspace. In a CSV, prefix any cell that starts with =, +, - or @ with an apostrophe, so a spreadsheet reads it as text rather than a formula.

**After the table, always add:**

- **Top outreach targets:** the top 3 to 5 survivors, one sentence each on why they go first.
- **Kills and parks:** each killed pursuit with its reason, each parked name with its revisit date.
- **Search parameters:** profile, partner types, geography, channels searched, target count, date generated.
- **Open questions:** anything you could not verify that the owner should look at.

When the investor channel ran, add the investor map, the per-portfolio play with its targets, and the monthly portfolio report when asked.

origin.heading: CSV — when >25 rows or user requests a file

sections.heading: ## Fallbacks
sections.text:
- Thin public data means a smaller list with the UNKNOWNs left visible, never padded out with guesses. If the count falls short of the target, say why.
- No enrichment integration: research public sources, starting with each firm's own site and about page. Slower, same bar.
- No portfolio data means building the investor map from owner knowledge marked INFERENCE, with enrichment as the first action.
- No warm path means the introduction ask gets drafted but never sent.

sections.heading: ## Self-check
sections.text:
Before handing back:

- [ ] Duplicates removed by domain.
- [ ] Every row has at least one source URL and a last verified date; every contact has its source URL and date.
- [ ] High confidence rests on two independent sources or the official page.
- [ ] Nothing came from bulk scraping, a bypassed wall, unprovenanced data, or a pattern-built address.
- [ ] Every top-tier line carries FACT, INFERENCE, or UNKNOWN, and no UNKNOWN is scored as a pass.
- [ ] Every kill has its reason and every park its revisit date.
- [ ] CSV cells starting with =, +, - or @ carry the apostrophe.
- [ ] The count matches the request, or the shortfall is explained.
- [ ] Nothing was sent to anyone.

ellis__c2-version-comparison.name: Contract version comparison
ellis__c2-version-comparison.description: Compare contract text without interpreting it: two drafts, a counterparty redline, a base agreement through every amendment, or a clause against your supplied approved text. Returns quote-exact Was/Now text with section cites, the latest text in document order, broken references and questions for counsel. Load when asked what changed between versions or amendments, or whether a clause matches approved wording.
triggers: does this clause match our approved wording

sections.text:
This file is a modified version of material licensed under Apache-2.0; see [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [ATTRIBUTION.md](ATTRIBUTION.md) in this package.

Loads two or more versions of contract text and shows exactly how they differ, in one of three modes: a summary of every change across a base agreement and its amendments, a trace of one provision to its latest text in document order, or a comparison of unsigned drafts, or of one clause against approved wording the user supplies. It quotes exact text with section cites and describes each change in neutral operational terms. It never decides which text controls, whether a change is acceptable, or what to do next; those go to counsel as questions.

sections.heading: ## When to use
## Inputs
sections.text:
Ask only for what is missing, in one message.

1. **Every version to compare**, complete, with the schedules, exhibits and definitions it refers to. Accept several files at once. If none are provided, ask.
2. **A name and version for each source**, such as "Base MSA, 1 March 2023", "Our draft v3" or "Counterparty markup, 12 May". Name each source and version before comparing.
3. **By mode:** for Mode 2, the provision to trace; for Mode 3, which version is ours and which is the counterparty's, or which is earlier.
4. **Optional:** an approved clause or playbook position, with its source. Without it there is no playbook column.
5. **Optional:** the named counsel or contract owner who will receive the questions.

sections.heading: ## Mode detection
sections.text:
Parse the user's request to determine which mode to run. Do not ask which mode unless the request is genuinely ambiguous.

**Mode 1 — Summary** (signed base agreement and amendments, no specific provision mentioned)
Trigger phrases: "what changed", "amendment history", "show me changes over time", "summarize amendments", "what does this contract look like now"

**Mode 2 — Provision trace** (specific clause or topic named)
Trigger phrases: "where's the [clause]", "latest [provision]", "how did [term] change", "find the indemnity", "what does it say now about [topic]"

**Mode 3 — Draft comparison** (unsigned versions: our draft against a counterparty markup, v1 against v2, or one clause against supplied approved text)
Trigger phrases: "compare these drafts", "what did they change in their markup", "redline comparison", "compare clauses", "does this clause match our approved wording". If the user names a clause, compare only that clause.

Common provision mappings:
- "indemnity" / "indemnification" → indemnification section
- "liability" / "liability cap" → limitation of liability
- "termination" → term and termination
- "data" / "privacy" / "DPA" → data protection provisions
- "IP" / "intellectual property" → IP ownership and licenses
- "price" / "fees" / "payment" → payment terms
- "auto-renewal" / "renewal" → renewal mechanics

If the term is ambiguous and maps to more than one provision, list the candidates and ask which one:
> "I found [N] provisions related to [term] — [list them]. Which one?"

If the overall request is ambiguous between modes, ask one question:
> "Summary of all changes across the contract, trace a specific provision — like indemnity, liability, or termination — or compare two drafts?"

sections.heading: ## Procedure
sections.text:
1. **Get the documents.** Take them from the chat (uploaded or pasted), from the workspace with `read_workspace_file`, or from Google Drive with `run_block`. If Drive is not connected, offer `connect_integration`, or ask for an upload or paste instead. Use only source text the user supplies.
2. **Detect the mode** (see Mode detection). Unsigned drafts, or a clause plus approved text, go to Mode 3, limited to the named clause if there is one. A clearly named provision in signed documents goes straight to Mode 2. Otherwise run Mode 1.
3. **Load and order the documents** (Step 1). If the order cannot be established from titles, dates or recitals, ask before reading content.
4. **Read and index** (Step 2).
5. **Compare literally** (Step 3), including the checklist.
6. **Write the output** in the template for the mode. Put the confidentiality line on top. Add the playbook column only if the user supplied approved text. End with questions for counsel.
7. **Run the self-check**, then return the result as a draft. Save it to the workspace with `write_workspace_file` only if the user asks. Do not email, share or post it.
8. **Offer follow-ups:**
   - "Want me to trace another provision?"
   - "Want a full playbook review of the current agreement as amended?" (routes to `nda-playbook-review` or `msa-playbook-review`, and needs the team's playbook)
   - "Want a brief for counsel on the open questions?" (routes to `counsel-escalation-brief`)

sections.heading: ## Step 1: Load and order the documents
sections.text:
In most cases the ordering is self-explanatory from document titles (e.g., "Amendment No. 1", "Second Amendment", "Addendum A") or dates visible in the filename or document header — proceed without asking.

Only ask the user to confirm ordering if:
- Filenames give no indication of sequence (e.g., "agreement-final.pdf", "agreement-v2.pdf", "agreement-markup.pdf")
- Dates are absent from both filenames and document headers
- Two documents appear to be the same amendment version

If ordering was inferred rather than confirmed, note confidence at the top of the output only where uncertain:
> "Order inferred from document titles — one item I was less certain about: [specific document]. Confirm if this affects your review."

**Ordering rules:**
- Always establish chronological order before reading content.
- If execution dates are available in metadata, use them.
- If not, look for dates in the document header or recitals ("This Amendment, dated as of...").
- Amendments often reference the agreement they modify ("this Amendment to the Master Services Agreement dated [X]") — use these references to confirm the chain.
- For Mode 3 drafts, label each version by its source (ours or counterparty) and its version or date.

origin.heading: Step 1: Load and order the documents

sections.heading: ## Step 2: Read and index
sections.text:
Read each document in order. For each, extract:
- Document type (base agreement, amendment number, addendum, draft or markup)
- Execution date, or version date for a draft
- Parties (confirm they match across documents — flag if a new party was added or a party name changed)
- A list of provisions explicitly modified, added, or deleted

Build a working index before producing output. Use it internally to drive the output — do not show it to the user.

sections.heading: ## Step 3: Compare literally
## Mode 1: Summary of all changes
sections.text:
```markdown
[Confidentiality line]

# Amendment History: [Counterparty] — [Agreement type]

**Base agreement:** [date]
**Amendments:** [N] ([date of first] → [date of last])
**Last amended:** [date]

## What changed — chronological

### Amendment 1 — [date]
**Purpose:** [one sentence from the recitals. If not stated, omit rather than guess.]

**Changes:**
- [Provision] (§[X.X]): Changed. Was: "[exact quote]" Now: "[exact quote]"
  Effect: [neutral operational effect]
- [New provision added] (§[X.X]): Added. Now: "[exact quote]"
- [Provision deleted] (§[X.X]): Deleted. Was: "[exact quote]"

### Amendment 2 — [date]
[same structure; repeat for each amendment]

## Net current state
Latest text in document order. Which text controls in a conflict is a question for counsel.

| Provision | Latest text | §Ref | Last changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| [clause] | "[exact quote; mark any omission with …]" | §[X.X] | Amendment N, [date] |
| [clause] | Unchanged from base: "[exact quote]" | §[X.X] | Base agreement |

## Watch items
[Flag anything that looks inconsistent — e.g., an amendment modifying a provision that was already deleted, contradictory language between amendments, a party name that changed without a formal assignment, or a provision where the section number shifted across documents. Add every Step 3 checklist finding. Include section references on every flag.]

## Questions for counsel
- [Exact question, with § refs and the quoted text it turns on]
```

sections.heading: ## Mode 2: Provision trace
sections.text:
Show only what changed. Do not list amendments where the provision was untouched — skip them entirely.

```markdown
[Confidentiality line]

# Provision Trace: [Provision name]
## [Counterparty] — [Agreement type]

### Original — [Base agreement date], §[X.X]
> "[exact quote]"

### Amendment [N] — [date], §[X.X]
**Was:**
> "[exact quote of prior language]"

**Now:**
> "[exact quote of replacement language]"

*What changed:* [one sentence — neutral operational effect]

[Only subsequent amendments that touched this provision appear here. All others are omitted.]

## Latest text in document order
**§[X.X] — [source document, date]**
> "[exact quote]"

Which text controls if documents conflict is a question for counsel.

## Watch items
[Flags, inconsistencies, open questions — with section references. Common items to check: whether the provision is subject to or carved out of the liability cap; whether the section number shifted across amendments; whether the amendment language conflicts with another provision. Add every Step 3 checklist finding.]

## Questions for counsel
- [Exact question, with § refs]
```

If the provision was never amended after the base agreement:
> "No amendment supplied modifies this provision. Latest text in document order: §[X.X], base agreement, [date]."

sections.heading: ## Mode 3: Draft comparison
sections.text:
```markdown
[Confidentiality line]

# Draft Comparison: [Agreement or clause] — [Version A] vs [Version B]

**Version A:** [name, ours or counterparty, version or date]
**Version B:** [name, ours or counterparty, version or date]
**Scope:** [whole draft | §§ compared]

| § | Version A | Version B | Change | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [X.X] | "[exact quote]" | "[exact quote]" | Added / Removed / Changed | [neutral operational effect] |

**Identical wording:** §§ [list]

## Checklist findings
- Defined terms added, removed or changed: [§ refs and quotes, or "none found"]
- Dates, amounts, periods, parties, standards, exceptions changed: [...]
- Cross-references that no longer resolve: [...]
- Cannot compare — schedule or definition missing: [...]

## Questions for counsel
- [Exact question, with § refs]
```

sections.heading: ## Playbook column (optional)
sections.text:
Use it only when the user supplies an approved clause or playbook position. Show the supplied text, with its source, in a separate column and label each item `MATCH`, `DEVIATION`, `MISSING` or `UNCLEAR`. In Mode 3 add the columns to the table; in Mode 2 add them under "Latest text in document order"; in Mode 1 add them to the Net current state table for the provisions the supplied text covers. For one clause against approved text with no second version, run Mode 3 with the agreement text as the only version column.

If no approved text is supplied, report only the version difference and never use those labels as a policy judgment. Never build an approved position from another contract or general practice.

Scope: single clauses, and agreement types that `nda-playbook-review` and `msa-playbook-review` do not cover. A whole NDA or MSA against a playbook goes to those skills.

sections.heading: ## Confidentiality
sections.text:
The source documents are often confidential in their own right and are typically read for counsel's analysis. Put this line at the top of every output:

> Confidential — contract text comparison prepared for counsel review. No legal advice or recommendation given. Do not forward.

Do not state that the output is privileged; that is counsel's call. Distribute it only within the group counsel names, and store it where privileged materials live. Strip the line before any external delivery.

sections.heading: ## What this skill does not do
sections.text:
- It does not determine which document controls in the event of a conflict between the base agreement and an amendment, or between drafts — that is a legal interpretation question. It flags conflicts and routes them to counsel as questions.
- It does not draft new amendments.
- It does not create a redline unless counsel supplies or approves the replacement text, and it never sends one.
- It does not review a whole NDA or MSA against a playbook; that is `nda-playbook-review` or `msa-playbook-review`.
- It does not infer what an amendment means if the language is ambiguous — it quotes exactly and flags ambiguity for counsel.
- It does not accept language, negotiate, approve, sign, or send anything. Any outward step waits for the user's approval.

origin.heading: What this skill does not do

sections.heading: ## Self-check
sections.text:
Before returning, confirm:
- Every document is named with its version and date, in the order used, and any inferred order is flagged.
- Every finding has a section reference and exact quoted text.
- Only identical wording is reported as unchanged.
- Every changed pair and watch item was run through the Step 3 checklist.
- Effects are neutral and operational, and nothing says which text controls.
- `MATCH`, `DEVIATION`, `MISSING` and `UNCLEAR` appear only beside supplied approved text.
- The confidentiality line is on top, the output ends with questions for counsel, and nothing was sent.

alex__roadmap.name: Product roadmap and prioritization
alex__roadmap.description: Use when the user hands over a backlog or competing priorities, asks what to build next, or needs the roadmap changed: RICE-scored items with sourced inputs, a capacity-checked now-next-later with owners and dependencies, a cut list, a dated change log, and the shipped-slipped-stuck review.

sections.heading: # Product roadmap and prioritization
sections.text:
Use this when the user hands over a backlog, a list of requests, or competing
priorities, or asks what to build next. Also use it when a roadmap already
exists and something has to change (an item added, a status changed, a date
moved, the order reshuffled), and to run the periodic review of roadmap
commitments against what actually happened.

The roadmap is the one record of what the team has committed to. Nothing lands
on it, and no date or scope is promised to anyone, without a yes from the
decision maker.

sections.heading: ## What you need first
sections.text:
The candidate items, the goal they serve, any dates already promised, and the
team's real capacity. No goal means you pick the sharpest one you hear and
mark it INFERENCE. No effort sizes means you score with rough person-month
bands and flag sizing as the first ask of the team.

Where the current roadmap comes from:

- Check connected sources first and never re-ask for one already connected. A
  tracker reachable through `run_block` (Linear, GitHub, Notion, Airtable,
  Google Sheets) or a connected MCP server gives the items with status, owner
  and dates. Note what is overdue, at risk, or recently completed, and surface
  any item without a clear owner or date.
- Nothing connected: ask for the roadmap or backlog pasted or uploaded in any
  form (list, table, spreadsheet, screenshot, prose). A CSV works just as well.
- For a change or a review, read the last saved dated roadmap. It is what the
  change log diffs against. If there is no earlier save, say this run is the
  baseline.

Ask for whatever is missing one question at a time.

sections.heading: ## Pick the mode
sections.text:
Infer the mode from the request. Ask one question only when the request
genuinely leaves it open.

- A backlog, a pile of requests, or a roadmap to build from scratch: go to
  **Score, cut, order**.
- An existing roadmap with something to add, re-status, move, or reorder: go
  to **Change the roadmap**.
- What shipped, slipped, or is stuck, or the weekly product review: go to
  **Review the commitments**.
- Whether to build something at all, or which direction to take: hand it to
  product strategy and bets (`product-strategy-and-bets`). This skill orders
  work; it does not pick the bet.

sections.heading: ## Score, cut, order
sections.text:
1. Write each candidate as one line: the user, the job, the outcome. Anything
   you cannot phrase that way goes back to the user as a question, not onto
   the roadmap.
2. Score every item on reach, impact, confidence, and effort, the RICE model:
   score = (reach x impact x confidence) / effort. Reach is customers per
   cycle from real metrics. Impact is 0.25 / 0.5 / 1 / 2 / 3 on how much it
   moves the goal. Confidence is 100% / 80% / 50% on the estimates behind it.
   Effort is person-months across product, design, and engineering in whole
   numbers, minimum 0.5. Show the score and a one-line reason beside each, so
   the ordering can be argued with. Evidence grades stay in the reason line,
   not inside confidence. Run the arithmetic with `bash_exec` rather than by
   eye.
   - **No reach data?** Fall back to ICE or a value-vs-effort placement
     (`references/prioritization-methods.md`). Label those scores INFERENCE,
     name the method on the output, and keep the same method across updates.
3. Cut before you order. Kill duplicates, fold near-duplicates, and park
   anything that serves no goal. The cut list carries reasons, and nothing cut
   returns without new evidence.
4. Map dependencies before you order. For each survivor, name what it waits
   on (technical, team, external, knowledge, or sequential), with an owner, a
   need-by date, and a contingency if it slips. A need-by date nobody has
   given is UNKNOWN. Prerequisites land ahead of the items that need them.
   Types, buffers, and ways to remove a dependency are in
   `references/dependencies-and-capacity.md`.
5. Lay the survivors into now, next, and later. Now holds only what fits this
   cycle, with named owners. Later is not a graveyard: each item keeps the
   trigger that would promote it.
6. Check capacity against the team they named. Capacity is people times the
   period, less known overhead, in person-months so it compares with effort.
   Without the team's own figures, use the rules of thumb and label them
   INFERENCE: 60-70% of engineering time goes to planned feature work, split
   by default 70% planned features, 20% technical health, 10% unplanned
   (`references/dependencies-and-capacity.md`). If now exceeds it, say what
   drops and ask. Never silently overload the cycle; cut scope rather than
   pretend people can do more.

sections.heading: ## Change the roadmap
sections.text:
Read the last saved dated roadmap first, then run the operation the request
names:

- **Add item.** Gather the goal it serves, the owner, and its dependencies.
  Phrase and score it like any other item, with the same method, and suggest
  where it fits against current priorities and capacity. Always ask: what
  comes off? The roadmap is zero-sum against capacity.
- **Update status.** Not started, in progress, at risk, blocked, completed, or
  cut. At risk or blocked needs the blocker and the mitigation plan; ask for
  whichever is missing.
- **Move timeline.** Ask why: scope change, dependency slip, or resource
  constraint. Walk the dependent items for downstream impact and flag any item
  that moves past a hard deadline. A new date is a proposal until the decision
  maker approves it.
- **Reprioritize.** Ask what changed: new information, a strategy shift, a
  resource change, or customer feedback. Priority follows new information, not
  whim. Re-score with the same method and show a before/after table.

Then, for every change:

1. Hold the threshold. Not every piece of news changes the roadmap: batch
   changes at the team's cadence unless something is truly urgent, and keep
   scope adjustments apart from real reprioritization.
2. Write **Changes this update** against the last saved version: added,
   removed, reprioritized, timeline shifts, status changes, each with its
   date and reason.
3. If the change moves or drops something someone was expecting, draft the
   change note: acknowledge the change, the reason, the trade-off, the new
   plan, and who is affected. It stays a draft until the owner says yes to
   sending it.

Formats for the change log, the before/after table, and the note are in
`references/change-communication.md`.

sections.heading: ## Review the commitments
sections.text:
When the ask is a review rather than a fresh ordering: read the roadmap, the
scored backlog, and the last review, and log what you could not reach. Open
with one line — the period, and how many now-items shipped, slipped, or went
quiet. Then three short blocks: shipped; slipped, with the reason and the new
date; stuck, with the owner and the unblock ask. Score each commitment red,
yellow, or green — a slip with no new date is red. Show the same fixed KPI
table every time; never drop a metric because it looks bad. End with the
forward half: asks, each a decision needed from a named person by a date, and
three to five outcome-led commitments for the next period, plus the one call
the period needs, written so the decision maker can answer yes or no. Keep a
log of reviewed items so the same stuck thing is never re-flagged without
saying what changed since.

sections.heading: ## Output
sections.text:
The scored list, the now-next-later roadmap with owners and dependencies, and
the cut list with reasons — saved dated. Report the top three and the first
cut in the chat; the full sheet lives where the team reads it. File now-items
as tickets only on a yes. A period where everything is on track is three lines
saying so, not a report.

The saved sheet holds:

- **Scored list**: each item as user, job, outcome; its inputs and score; the
  method used; the one-line reason with its FACT, INFERENCE, or UNKNOWN label.
- **Roadmap**: now, next, later, each item with owner, status, and what it
  depends on; later items with their promotion trigger; a date only where the
  decision maker approved one. Marked draft until that yes.
- **Cut list**: each item with its reason.
- **Capacity check**: available person-months against the effort in now, and
  what drops if it does not fit.
- **Changes this update** (any change after the first save), plus the drafted
  change note when someone is affected.

sections.heading: ## When the sizing is guesswork
sections.text:
Scores are not a hard rule: a dependency or a table-stakes bet may jump the
order with a dated reason naming the trade-off. Never promise a date or a
scope the decision maker did not approve, and never reorder silently after a
review — every change gets a dated note.

sections.heading: ## Guardrails
sections.text:
- Draft first, then name the exact ask and wait. Filing tickets, changing
  tracker statuses, and sending a change note to anyone each need the owner's
  yes to that specific thing.
- Label every load-bearing claim FACT, INFERENCE, or UNKNOWN. A reach number
  with no source and no period is not quoted. Never invent a metric, a
  customer, a date, or a commitment.
- Stay on ordering. A build decision goes to PRD and acceptance criteria
  (`product-prd-and-acceptance-criteria`); what users said goes to discovery
  and user research (`product-discovery-and-user-research`); an exec, board,
  or steering version goes to product exec briefing (`product-exec-briefing`).

sections.heading: ## Self-check
sections.text:
- Every item is one line of user, job, outcome, with a score, a named method,
  and a labelled reason.
- The cut list has reasons; every later item has a promotion trigger.
- Every dependency has an owner, a need-by date or UNKNOWN, and a contingency;
  no item sits ahead of its prerequisite.
- Now fits the stated capacity, or the drop question has been asked.
- A change carries its dated entry in Changes this update; a reprioritize
  carries the before/after table.
- Nothing was filed, sent, or promised without a yes.

sections.heading: ## References
sections.text:
- `references/dependencies-and-capacity.md`: dependency types and handling,
  capacity estimates and allocation.
- `references/prioritization-methods.md`: ICE and value-vs-effort fallbacks,
  now-next-later horizons, other views of the same roadmap.
- `references/change-communication.md`: change triggers, the whiplash
  threshold, the change log and before/after formats, the change note.

Portions of this package are adapted under Apache-2.0; see `ATTRIBUTION.md`
and `LICENSE`.

casey__test-planning.name: Test plan draft
casey__test-planning.description: Plan tests for one change, or the test approach for a new service or component, from risk: failure modes with who they hurt, cases in risk order with data, level and existing coverage, exit criteria, and the gaps someone must accept. Load it when asked what to test before a merge or release, for a test or QA plan, or how to test a new component. Drafts only; never marks a case passed.

sections.heading: # Test plan draft
sections.text:
Use this for a feature, fix, or refactor before it is merged or released. Also
use it for the test approach to a new service or component, even when only a
design doc exists.

Not for writing or changing test code, reviewing a diff for bugs
(pull-request-review), or making the release call (release-readiness-checklist,
which takes this plan's exit criteria).

sections.heading: ## Inputs
sections.text:
Ask for what is missing in one `ask_question`:

- **The change**: the pull request or diff. Read it, and the code it touches,
  through the GitHub blocks (`run_block`). If GitHub is not connected, offer
  `connect_integration`, or ask for the pasted diff and the changed file names.
- **What it should do**: the requirement, ticket, or acceptance criteria.
- **Existing tests**: the test files near the change, read through GitHub or
  pasted, and a coverage report if the team has one.
- **Environments**: where tests can run (local, CI, staging) and which of these
  do not exist.
- **Release date**: when it merges or ships.
- **New component only**: the design doc, the component type, and who consumes
  its interface.

If an earlier setup brief (code-quality-getting-started) or the team's test
conventions are in memory (`memory_search`), start from them instead of asking
again.

Only a description, no code: plan from the description and acceptance
criteria, mark every existing-coverage field `unknown`, and list "code not
read" as the first gap.

sections.heading: ## Procedure
sections.text: Work in order. Step 1 sets the mode; steps 2 to 7 are the same for both.

sections.heading: ### 1. Choose the mode
sections.text:
- **Change mode**: a feature, fix, or refactor with a diff, a pull request, or
  a clear description. Go to step 2.
- **New component mode**: a new service or component, often with no code yet.
  Load `references/strategy-by-component.md`, place each part of the design in
  it (API endpoints, data pipelines, frontend, infrastructure), and record the
  test types each part needs, the environment each would run in, and the
  consumers that need contract tests. Then run steps 2 to 7 on the component's
  main flows. A test type with no environment to run in becomes a gap in
  step 6.
- **Both** (a change that adds a new component): do the component view first,
  then the change.

sections.heading: ### 2. List what can break
sections.text:
From the change and the code around it, list the ways it can fail: wrong
output, bad input, empty or large data, permissions, security boundaries, data
integrity, concurrency, time zones, retries, and old data. For each, note who
it hurts and how it would be noticed.

Where the change touches them, add non-functional and deployment risks:
performance, accessibility, feature flags in both the on and off state,
migrations and backward compatibility, and rollback.

When a failure mode comes from reading the code, name the file and line. When
it comes only from the description, say so.

sections.heading: ### 3. Rank the risks
sections.text:
Rate each failure mode's likelihood and impact as high, medium, or low, each
with a one-line reason. Order the list by likelihood x impact, highest first;
this is the risk order the later steps use. A failure mode you cannot rate
stays `unknown` and visible; do not fold it into low.

sections.heading: ### 4. Cases and data
sections.text:
Write the cases in risk order. For each give:

- an ID and the priority from step 3;
- what it checks and the risk it covers;
- setup and test data;
- steps and expected result;
- level: unit, integration, end-to-end, or manual;
- whether an existing test already covers it.

Prefer a few cases that catch real failures over many that repeat the happy
path. Choose the lowest level that catches the risk, trading confidence against
speed and flakiness, and keep end-to-end cases few; this is a heuristic, not a
quota. Skip trivial getters and setters, framework code, and one-off scripts.

Pick the inputs with `references/test-design-techniques.md`: boundary values,
equivalence classes, state transitions, and pairwise combinations.

For existing coverage, name the test file and test you read. Write `covered`
only when you saw that test pass in a run you were shown; otherwise write
`test exists, not seen run`, `none found`, or `unknown` (tests not read).

Use synthetic or anonymised test data only. Never copy production personal data
into fixtures, and say where each data set comes from.

sections.heading: ### 5. Exit criteria
sections.text:
State what must be true before merge and before release: which case IDs must
pass, at which level, in which environment, and who runs them. List any open
bug allowed to ship and who must accept it. These criteria are what
release-readiness-checklist checks the evidence against. Add a coverage
percentage only if the team already sets one; never propose one.

sections.heading: ### 6. Coverage gaps
sections.text:
List what the plan does not cover and why: no test data, no environment, cost,
or low risk. Name who should accept each gap. Include every `unknown` risk
from step 3 and every test type from step 1 with no environment to run in. If you
do not know who owns a gap, name the role and ask.

sections.heading: ### 7. Draft and hand over
sections.text:
Fill `templates/test-plan.md` and return it as a draft. Offer to save it to the
workspace (`write_workspace_file`). If the user wants the cases filed as
tickets or the plan posted on the pull request, show exactly what will be
created and wait for their approval before anything is written outside the
chat.

sections.heading: ## Output
sections.text:
One test plan in the shape of `templates/test-plan.md`:

1. Summary: the change or component, the mode, what was read and what was not,
   and the merge or release date.
2. Test types by part (new component mode only): part, component type, test
   types, environment, contract consumers.
3. Risks in risk order: failure mode, who it hurts, how it would be noticed,
   likelihood, impact, and the file and line or "description only".
4. Cases in risk order: ID, risk, what it checks, level, setup and data, steps,
   expected result, existing coverage, priority, and status `not run`.
5. Exit criteria for merge and for release.
6. Gaps: what is not covered, why, and who should accept it.

sections.heading: ## Guardrails
sections.text:
Never mark a case as passed or covered without seeing it run. Do not change
the test suite, skip a test, or merge anything; the team decides which cases to
build.

- Never invent an existing test, a coverage figure, or a failure the code does
  not support. Say whether each point was read in the code, taken from the
  description, or assumed.
- No coverage percentage targets unless the team supplies them.
- Synthetic or anonymised test data only.
- This skill plans; writing the tests is a separate job.
- Nothing is written outside the chat (tickets, comments, docs) without the
  user's approval of the exact draft.

sections.heading: ## Self-check
sections.text:
- Every risk says who it hurts, how it would be noticed, and where it came from.
- Cases are in risk order, and each has data, steps, expected result, level,
  and existing coverage.
- No case says passed, and none says covered without a run you saw.
- No invented coverage target; all test data is synthetic or anonymised.
- Exit criteria name case IDs and environments.
- Every gap has a reason and someone to accept it.

sections.heading: ## Files
sections.text:
- `templates/test-plan.md`: the output shape; fill it every time.
- `references/test-design-techniques.md`: how to pick inputs (step 4).
- `references/strategy-by-component.md`: test types per component type (new
  component mode, step 1).
- `LICENSE` and `ATTRIBUTION.md`: the licence and source record for the
  adapted component list and the focus, skip, and level notes in steps 2 and 4.

anika__c4-partner-enablement-kit.name: Onboard and enable partners
anika__c4-partner-enablement-kit.description: Use when a partner agreement is signed: run the 30/60/90 onboarding arc, build the partner-seller kit (pitch sheet, objections, demo script, ROI inputs, case briefs) tiered by model with sourced proof only, and plan the first co-marketing motion.

sections.heading: # Onboard and enable partners
sections.text:
Use this when an agreement is signed. It runs the 30/60/90 onboarding
arc, stands up the kit the partner's sellers will use, and plans the first
co-marketing motion.

The kit is for the partner's sellers. Collateral for our own direct sales
team is out of scope: name it and hand it back.

sections.heading: ## Inputs
sections.text:
Check what is already connected (CRM, partner portal, learning system,
calendar, documents) before asking. Ask one question at a time, and never
ask twice for something already linked.

- The partner and the agreement model: referral, reseller, co-sell, or
  managed service provider / systems integrator (MSP/SI).
- The signature date, and the owner's timezone for every date.
- The named owner on each side.
- Portal and training access: what exists and who has logins.
- The first joint motion.
- For the kit: the product claims and differentiators the owner has
  approved, the customer proof you can cite (case-study files, CRM
  records, call transcripts, quotes with their source), what materials
  exist today, and what partner sellers ask for most.
- The objections partner sellers hear most, and the top competitor for the
  battle card.

A missing input does not stop the work. Name the gap at the top, mark every
assumption as an assumption, and carry on with what is there.

origin.heading: Stand up the kit, tiered by model

sections.heading: ## Procedure
sections.text:
1. **Confirm the trigger.** No signed agreement means stop and route to
   structure-the-partner-agreement. An ask for our own direct sellers goes
   back to the owner.
2. **Book the kickoff inside five business days of signature**, then set
   the arc (see "Start inside five business days"). If the kickoff cannot
   land inside five business days, say so at the top with the reason.
3. **Pick the kit tier from the agreement model** (see "Stand up the kit,
   tiered by model").
4. **Draft each kit item.** The pitch sheet, top three objections, demo
   script, ROI inputs and case briefs follow
   [references/partner-kit-templates.md](references/partner-kit-templates.md).
   No citable proof for a slot means it ships as
   `UNKNOWN — needs: <record>`. Do not hold the kit back and do not fill
   the gap.
5. **Set certification and refresh rules.** Take the certification ladder
   from build-partner-academies-at-scale. No ladder set yet means asking
   the owner or running that skill first; never make up pass bars.
6. **Plan the first co-marketing motion** (see "Plan the first co-marketing
   motion"). A campaign calendar beyond this first item goes to
   run-the-partner-marketing-engine.
7. **Schedule the health checks** at each 30-day mark. Offer to set them as
   follow-ups; set them only on your yes.
8. **Stage everything as a draft.** Hand back the package below, name what
   each partner-facing item asks the partner for, and wait for your yes
   before anything leaves. Log the dated draft.

origin.heading: Stand up the kit, tiered by model

sections.heading: ## Start inside five business days
sections.text:
Enablement starts within five business days of signature with a Day 1-5
kickoff: a timed two-hour agenda covering introductions, goals, access,
and the first motion.

Then set the arc and file it where the owner actually looks:

- Days 0-30: discovery, portal access, core training, the welcome package
  (guide, contacts, logins, incentives), and a co-authored joint business
  plan — why, goals, benchmarks, how the two sides work, how success gets
  measured.
- Days 31-60: certification or shadowed calls, plus the first joint
  demand motion.
- Days 61-90: the first joint win, a pipeline review, and the
  next-quarter plan.
- Month 6: an independence check — are they selling without training
  wheels.
- Month 12: a plan revisit with year-two goals.

One owner on each side. Every milestone dated.

sections.heading: ## Stand up the kit, tiered by model
sections.text:
The full kit is: a pitch sheet their sellers can use this week, a battle
card against the top competitor (Legal-reviewed), a demo script, a
return-on-investment (ROI) calculator built on the ROI inputs, case briefs,
an FAQ, a security pack, three qualifying questions with exact wording, the
top three objections with a one-paragraph answer each, and training with
tiered certifications on the ladder that build-partner-academies-at-scale
defines.

| Model | Kit |
|-------|-----|
| Referral | A one-pager: the pitch sheet. |
| Reseller | The full playbook: the full kit above. |
| Co-sell | The full kit, plus an NFR (not-for-resale) or demo environment for their sellers. Only certified sellers lead co-sell; the rules on who leads each deal live in run-the-partner-co-sell-cadence. |
| MSP/SI | The full kit, plus an NFR or demo environment, technical certification for the people who deliver, and a delivery-readiness check before client work (the readiness rubric lives in build-partner-academies-at-scale). |

Each artifact names its owner and its refresh date, and refreshes inside
five days of any release. Name the response SLA for partner requests while
you are at it.

sections.heading: ## Plan the first co-marketing motion
sections.text:
One dated item — a webinar, a joint post, or an event — with who brings
the audience, who makes the asset, and how spend and market development
fund (MDF) claims work.

Check the MDF fiscal-year expiry. Fund rules and reallocation belong to
design-the-partner-program. Any spend commitment or MDF allocation is
staged as a draft for your yes. An undated idea stays a backlog line, never
a commitment.

sections.heading: ## Run the health checks
sections.text:
At each 30-day mark: milestones hit, certification progress, first
pipeline. A miss gets a dated rescue line with an owner, not silence.

sections.heading: ## What you hand back
sections.text:
- The 90-day arc with owners and dates, plus the month-6 and month-12
  checks.
- The enablement kit list for the partner's model, with each item's owner
  and refresh date.
- The drafted kit items in the working form the templates name, with every
  metric and quote carrying its source or marked UNKNOWN, and a short list
  of the records that would fill each UNKNOWN.
- The first co-marketing item.
- The health-check schedule.
- At the top: access gaps, assumptions, and the partner-facing items
  waiting for your yes.

sections.heading: ## Guardrails
sections.text:
- Nothing partner-facing leaves without your yes: not the welcome package,
  the plan, the kit, or training content. No posting to shared channels and
  no fund claims on anyone's behalf.
- Spend, MDF allocations and incentives are never committed here. They are
  staged as drafts with their evidence.
- Never invent a number, a person, a title, a date, a quote, or a
  commitment. Label each load-bearing claim FACT, INFERENCE or UNKNOWN with
  its source. An unverified metric stays UNKNOWN, never zero.
- The partner's claims stay in their own words, beside ours. Partner names,
  titles and numbers stay exactly as the source wrote them.
- The battle card is Legal-reviewed before it ships.

origin.heading: Stand up the kit, tiered by model

sections.heading: ## Fallbacks
sections.text:
No portal or learning system yet means the arc runs on documents and live
sessions, and you name the access gap at the top. No connected documents
or sheets means writing the kit as workspace files. No CRM connection means
asking for an export or a paste. No approved proof yet means the kit ships
with its UNKNOWN slots showing.

sections.heading: ## Self-check
sections.text:
- Is the kickoff inside five business days of signature, or is the slip
  named?
- Does every milestone have a date and an owner on each side?
- Does the kit match the model's row?
- Does every metric and quote carry a source, or read UNKNOWN with the
  record that would fill it?
- Did every certification pass bar come from the ladder or the owner?
- Is the co-marketing item dated, with spend and MDF lines awaiting your
  yes?
- Is every partner-facing item marked as a draft?

frankie__meeting-brief.name: Meeting prep brief
frankie__meeting-brief.description: Use before a named meeting or for every meeting on a day: a one-page brief led by the outcome needed, then logistics, attendees, last contact, open items with owners, pre-reads and questions, each fact sourced and dated, with extra prep for deal, board, vendor and regulatory meetings. Not for sales calls on a live deal.

sections.heading: # Meeting prep brief
sections.text:
Prepare a one-page brief for a meeting: the decision or outcome needed,
purpose, people, history, open items and pre-reads, with every fact sourced
and dated.

sections.heading: ## When to use
sections.text:
Use this before a named meeting, or for every meeting on a given day.

Use something else when:

- the meeting is a sales call on a live deal: use `sales-call-preparation`;
- the meeting has already happened and the job is action items, owners and
  dates, or a recap: use `meeting-follow-up-draft`;
- the ask is a board or investor metrics pack rather than a brief for the
  meeting: use `board-and-investor-metrics-brief`.

sections.heading: ## Inputs
sections.text:
Take what the request and the invite already give you. Ask only for what is
still missing, all in one `ask_question`:

- **Meeting**: which one (title and date), or which day.
- **Meeting type**: deal review, board or committee, vendor call, team sync,
  client or customer, regulatory or government, litigation or dispute,
  cross-functional, or other.
- **The principal's role**: advisor, presenter, negotiator or observer.
- **Preparation time available**: how long there is before the meeting, so the
  gathering fits it.

If a source is not connected, the principal can paste the invite or agenda, or
upload a file, instead.

sections.heading: ## Procedure
sections.text: Work through these steps in order.

sections.heading: ### 1. Find the meeting
sections.text:
- **A named meeting**: find the invite in Google Calendar through `run_block`.
- **A whole day**: read that day's events and brief each meeting in time order.
- **Calendar not connected**: say so once, offer `connect_integration`, and
  work from a pasted invite or agenda or an uploaded file
  (`read_workspace_file`) meanwhile.
- **The meeting has already ended**: stop and offer `meeting-follow-up-draft`.
- **Two contacts share a name**: confirm which one before going on.

sections.heading: ### 2. Fill the intake gaps
sections.text:
If the invite does not show the meeting type, the principal's role or the time
available, ask for them together in one `ask_question` (see Inputs). Do not
ask for anything the invite already answers.

sections.heading: ### 3. Match the meeting type
sections.text:
If the meeting is a deal review, board or committee, vendor call, team sync,
client or customer, regulatory or government, litigation or dispute, or
cross-functional meeting, open
[references/meeting-types.md](references/meeting-types.md). Add that type's
prep needs to what you gather in step 4, and its extra sections to the brief.
Otherwise write the standard brief.

sections.heading: ### 4. Gather the context
sections.text:
Collect the purpose, the attendees and their roles, the last time the
principal met them, what was agreed then, and anything promised since. Note
the source and date of each fact. Search only threads about this meeting's
subject.

| Source | Through | What to pull |
|---|---|---|
| Google Calendar | `run_block` | Time, length, place or link, attendees; prior meetings with the same attendees in the last 3 months; related follow-ups already scheduled; competing commitments |
| Gmail | `run_block` | Recent threads with or about the attendees on this subject; earlier follow-up threads and the open action items in them; documents shared by email |
| Slack | `run_block` | Recent discussion of the meeting topic; decisions or context shared in channels |
| Google Drive | `run_block` | The agenda, prior meeting notes, shared documents and draft materials |
| HubSpot | `run_block` | Account or deal stage, relationship history, stakeholder map |
| The web | `web_search` | Public background on external attendees and their organisations |
| The principal | paste or upload | An invite, agenda or notes, when a source above is not connected |

If a source is not connected, offer `connect_integration` once, carry on with
the rest, and list it under Gaps.

origin.heading: Step 3: Gather Context from Connected Sources

sections.heading: ### 5. Screen for legal stakes
### 6. Write the brief
sections.text:
Write to the output contract below, on one page. Then:

- **Presenter or negotiator**: add Talking points, two or three, each tied to a
  sourced open item.
- **Negotiator**: add Red lines only from a playbook the principal supplied or
  a counsel instruction, quoted with its source. Otherwise write
  "UNKNOWN - confirm with counsel".
- **Questions**: list two or three questions that would move the decision on,
  drawn from the open items. Note any topic the principal said to avoid.

sections.heading: ### 7. Close with gaps and hand over
sections.text:
End with the Gaps block: sources not connected, information that looks
outdated, questions still open, and documents not found. Give the brief to the
principal only. Sharing it with attendees or anyone else, and any change to
the invite, waits for a clear yes.

sections.heading: ## Output contract
sections.text:
One page, in this order. Owners in bold, dates and times explicit, each fact
with its source and date. Mark anything you could not confirm, and leave out
private details from unrelated threads.

```text
Confidential - for <named readers> only           <- legal-stakes meetings only

1. Outcome needed: <one line; the summary for anyone with thirty seconds>
   Decision: <options on the table>; decides: **<owner>**   <- only when a decision is due
2. Logistics: <purpose> | <date, time, timezone> | <place or link> | <length>
   Your role: <advisor / presenter / negotiator / observer>
3. Attendees
   - <name>, <role, organisation>: <one line> (<source>, <date>)
4. Last time and open items
   - Agreed: <what> (<source>, <date>)
   - <open item>: **<owner>**, due <date> (<source>)
5. Read first
   - <document>: <link>

Talking points                                     <- presenter or negotiator only
   1. <point>: ties to <open item> (<source>)
Red lines                                          <- negotiator only; sourced, or UNKNOWN - confirm with counsel
Questions to ask
   - <question>: <why it moves the decision>
<Type> extras                                      <- from references/meeting-types.md
Gaps
   - Sources not connected: <...>
   - Looks outdated: <...>
   - Questions still open: <...>
   - Documents not found: <...>
```

sections.heading: ## Guardrails
sections.text:
- Never accept, decline, or move the meeting without a clear yes.
- Do not invent what someone said or agreed. Mark anything you could not
  confirm.
- Keep what you read private. Leave out private details from unrelated
  threads.
- The brief is for the principal. Sharing it, or sending anything to
  attendees, is drafted first and waits for approval.
- Talking points never promise a date, refund or policy exception on the
  company's behalf. Draft the commitment and flag it for the principal to
  approve.
- This is meeting preparation, not legal advice. Legal judgement, red lines,
  negotiation or litigation strategy and settlement parameters come only from
  counsel-supplied material; otherwise write "UNKNOWN - confirm with counsel".
- For a decision, show the options and who owns it. Do not recommend a legal
  position.

sections.heading: ## Self-check
sections.text:
- [ ] Item 1 states the outcome needed in one line.
- [ ] Every fact carries a source and a date; anything unconfirmed is marked.
- [ ] Every open item names its owner in bold.
- [ ] The legal-stakes screen ran: a confidential line where needed, and no
  legal point filled in without a counsel source.
- [ ] Gaps lists every source not connected and every document not found.
- [ ] Nothing was accepted, declined, moved, sent or shared.
